storylines.latest_title: Supercharging XLA-Based Inference: Announcing the Launch of XLA Serving Engine

prior_narrative.tldr: DeepSeek tied its V4.1-Flash model to its own agent harness on Oct 17, then on Oct 20 open-sourced DeepInfer, the inference engine behind its production services. On Oct 31 it published the architecture of an always-on coding agent, dsh-superagent.
prior_narrative.whats_new: Coverage of the dsh-superagent prototype, a router-worker coding agent that watches team chat for work, continued through Nov 4, while the rest of the thread is third-party inference-engine news.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: DeepSeek is releasing both the serving layer (DeepInfer, reportedly 155T tokens/day) and an agent harness, so platform teams can inspect a production-scale stack, but the cost and throughput figures come from DeepSeek and press reports, not independent benchmarks.

status.detail: Two DeepSeek open-source drops, DeepInfer and dsh-superagent, with no independent benchmarks yet.

beats.summary: Positioned against Claude Code; works from team chat.

beats.summary: llm-d 1.0, Nvidia Flare, XLA Serving Engine and hosting-profitability discussion.

open_questions: Will anyone publish independent throughput or cost benchmarks of DeepInfer outside DeepSeek's own figures?
Which models and hardware does DeepInfer support beyond DeepSeek's own?
Is dsh-superagent usable beyond a research prototype, and under what license?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: Before adopting DeepInfer or dsh-superagent, check license terms and hardware support, and benchmark them against your current serving stack rather than relying on the quoted token-per-day numbers.

storylines.label: Kimi K3.1
storylines.latest_title: Zero Mismatch, Simple Async RL: REINFORCE Zero, DeepSeek-V4.1 and Kimi K3.1

prior_narrative.tldr: Kimi K3.1 surfaced as an unreleased name after Arena testing, then Moonshot launched the roughly 3T-parameter K3.1 Pro on Oct 24. A quota-driven rocky rollout was followed by third-party hosting, vLLM day-0 support and, on Nov 5, full open weights.
prior_narrative.whats_new: vLLM's Nov 6 post uses Kimi K3.1 as a test case for zero-mismatch async RL, aligning rollout and training kernels bit for bit one day after the full weights shipped.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: K3.1 Pro is now self-hostable on vLLM and Ascend, and vLLM's RL work shows it is also a fine-tuning target. Licence terms and a 1.56TB footprint decide whether that beats third-party hosts or first-party quotas.

status.detail: K3.1 Pro moved from a quota-troubled first-party launch to third-party hosting, vLLM support and a full weights release; vLLM now documents RL training with it. Independent quality and cost data are still thin.

beats.summary: Moonshot releases the full 1.56TB, 2.8T-parameter weights with conditional commercial use; Huawei Ascend lists day-zero support.

beats.headline: vLLM applies zero-mismatch async RL to Kimi K3.1
beats.summary: vLLM describes aligning rollout and training kernels and unclipped importance sampling for stale-weight lag, covering DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, Kimi K3.1 and AMD MI355X.

open_questions: Do independent evals show K3.1 Pro matching Opus 5.5 on coding or agent tasks?
What do the commercial-use conditions in the weights licence actually restrict?
What do third-party hosts charge versus Moonshot's first-party plans and quotas?
Does anyone publish a K3.1 RL fine-tune that uses vLLM's zero-mismatch setup?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: Read the weights licence conditions before planning a self-host, and budget for 1.56TB of storage. Pin the vLLM version and rerun your own evals against Opus 5.5 before changing routing; for RL, check the bit-for-bit kernel alignment in vLLM's post first.
